newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Japan's Hashimoto breaks mould with dose of charm.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto breaks mould with dose of charm.

text.p: Japanese prime ministers have many qualities, but charm is not necessarily considered foremost among them.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, however, cracked the standard stiff mould during his two-day visit to Australia which ended on Tuesday, and some in New Zealand appeared to be anticipating more of the same.
"He is a man of great directness and humour," one senior New Zealand diplomat said ahead of Hashimoto's arrival.

Hashimoto, who arrived in Wellington late on Tuesday on the last leg of a diplomatic swing which has already taken him to Washington and Canberra, charmed his Australian hosts with an unexpected display of off-the-cuff wit.
Departing from a prepared policy speech at a dinner on Monday to ad-lib several jokes, Hashimoto drew laughter from his audience of Australian members of parliament and business leaders.
Many Japanese leaders are wary of taking such a relaxed and jovial approach to public diplomacy for fear of offending by mistake.

Hashimoto, however, appeared undaunted by such potential pitfalls, jesting, for example, that the high cost of Australian black opals -- one of which he purchased for his wife to mark their wedding anniversary on Sunday -- could be bad for the two-way trade gap.
He also confessed he had drunk too much to recall the label on the bottle of Australian wine that the couple shared en route to Australia to mark the event.

Some Australians were impressed with Hashimoto's suave and polished style. "(Prime Minister John) Howard's speech was warm, but boring," said one Australian official. "Hashimoto's very charismatic -- I wish we had some (politicians) like that."

Hashimoto also left at least some of his Australian observers with an impression he might well wish was shared by more of the folks back home -- that of a political leader who is not at the mercies of his bureaucratic mentors.
"Most Australians think that Japanese prime ministers are controlled by the bureaucrats, but he doesn't appear to be," the official said.
Hashimoto has pledged to enact six key domestic reforms, including cutting government agencies down to size and reducing the red tape that strangles Japanese business.
While he is generally perceived to be one of Japan's most assertive leaders, many critics worry that his close and long- standing ties with bureaucrats will undermine the impetus for reform.
Hashimoto will meet New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger and other members of Wellington's coalition cabinet on Wednesday before departing for Japan.
